utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, and Denise Gustin. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good afternoon to you, too. So Ms. Dresden is not here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She is in class, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any preliminaries? I see none. So usher, you can bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are proceeding with the -- with our questions, and we'll hope to finish with your testimony as early as possible today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your entry, diary entry of April 9, 1992, you put at the same level, you compare Glas with Goebbels' Volkischer Beobachter. Now, how familiar were you at the time with Goebbels' Volkischer Beobachter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I knew a great deal because I was interested in the topic. I've read a lot about the Third Reich, and I know quite a lot about it. I know what the Beobachter served ultimately. I am fully aware of what I said and of the comparison I made. Thanks to you, and thank you for having told me what your questions would be, I've reviewed my entries and highlighted some of them. Glas was a racist paper, and I claim this with responsibility. I can give you an illustration if you allow me, just two or three sentences. On the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I don't know whether you can see, but the witness has actually got a separate book with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. So if he can just identify where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you reading from? I can't see from here. Thanks for pointing that out, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are some annotations I make about things that I'm interested in, and this is a private notebook that I brought with me, but it relates to the period that you are questioning me about. And I will tell you what it is about, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what is it about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerns the topic of racism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- one moment. I'm going to stop you for a while. What notebook is this? When did you write this notebook? I mean when did you write these notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These notes were made a long time ago. This is a transcript from Glas of 2nd June 1992. Since I knew what you were going to ask me, I looked up this particular entry to serve as an illustration of what I've said, that this was a racist paper like Beobachter. So I just wanted to illustrate this in two sentences, and I will not be using this notebook afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I really want to know what that is, Your Honour. I mean, that's something new that's now apparently in addition to his diary that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mean, you didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We could have gone all day without this coming into Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't need to say it because I was anticipating. Forget the notebook, because otherwise we will get into an alley --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you know what's in that notebook in any case. Tell us from your memory without referring to the notebook because we will ask you for it, it will involve us into translations and this and that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to understand I'm not trying to put obstacles in your way, but I'm trying to be practical for the sake of everybody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were telling us that Glas you considered to be a racist paper. You were about to read from a -- a notebook of yours. You agreed to forget about that notebook, but you are going to tell us why in your opinion or why in your considered opinion Glas was a racist paper. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of an illustration, this is something I know by heart and I can quote almost Glas. On the 2nd of June, 1992, published under the column "Statements" under the heading "genetic material," I will paraphrase now, this is how it approximately went: The West, which has become degenerated and incestuous, wants to penetrate to the Balkans, and conquer us. And we, the Serbs we are such a good-looking, intelligent people, that we are not going to allow this. To characterise the west as an incestuous, degenerated entity, well, that's racism for me. That's the first thing I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, let's go back now to Goebbels' Beobachter. You liken Glas to the Beobachter because you consider them both to be racist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That the only reason why you draw this comparison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them are racist, full of hatred toward the other side, and besides Glas was a wartime bulletin, a war bulletin. Yesterday, if I'm not mistaken, you asked me about the boy who was beaten up and whose photographs I've shown to you, whether they wrote about him. No, these would not be the things that Glas would be writing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also, in the same entry of 9th April 1992, you also seem to hint that even Banja Luka Radio was more objective than Glas. Do you maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular moment, on that particular day, they were more objective, and this is what made me write this report about Beobachter. I was prompted by this report recounting this incident by the hydroelectric plant Jajce II. On this decisive day, on the 8th of April, the Jajce public security station police pulled over a bus at a checkpoint. Reportedly according to what was said in Glas, they killed six reservists and one of them was wounded. The Glas journalist wrote that they were ambushed, whereas the Banja Luka Radio reported that they were stopped at the checkpoint, and that an incident ensued. So there wasn't an ambush. It was a checkpoint like the ones you could find throughout our country in great numbers. So what was the truth? All of them had placed some sort of barricades or checkpoints and were stopping one another. So this was a civilian bus regularly travelling on the route Banja Luka/Bugojno. So when they were stopped at Jajce to check what they call the so-called Croat/Muslim coalition, the JNA reservists who were seated in the back seats of the bus opened fire. And the other side returned fire. Now, the Glas reported that they were ambushed, which wasn't true, and reported that the very morning of the incident, all the Serbs were dismissed from their jobs. So the Glas was in the service of misinforming the people and pulling them apart. Glas was used to voice open threats to Muslims and Croats. I can read out some of these to you. I have them here in my diary. Miodrag Susnica was killed. He was a man employed at the MUP, I believe. So some Serb anti-terrorist forces - which could not have been in existence, but this is what it said they were - they threatened that unless the murderers surrender themselves within 48 hours, and they knew that these alleged murderers were Croats and Muslims, so this constituted a threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I understood you well -- if I understood you well when you say that Banja Luka Radio was more objective, you were referring only to this --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But generally speaking now, leaving this particular incident apart, would you put Glas and Banja Luka at the same level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would. There's this youth show which starts out by saying: "Good afternoon. Here are three Chetnik women who are going to entertain you." You, as a viewer, a Croat, a Muslim, you could not really feel comfortable with that. And these things used to happen. For instance, Predrag Djurkovic, the famous presenter, Stojic, another one, their shows were far from alleviating the tensions and the fear, especially with regard to Muslims. And I have to emphasise this, Muslims are the greater victims of the war in Bosnia because they are the least responsible for everything that happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, my question finally would be would you consider Banja Luka Radio generally speaking to be also racist and full of hatred as you depicted, or as you described Glas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a large extent, although at certain stages the radio did try to ease the rhetorics that they used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now I refer you to your entry of the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm sorry. Judge Janu would like -- Judge Janu has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I know you couldn't read everything, but maybe you were familiar with magazine or daily paper Jasnost, Kozarski Vjesnik. If you know the level and style of information of those, could you compare it with the Glas? Was it the same level concerning the propaganda or was it worse or better, if you follow these two papers as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say I haven't had either of these magazines in my hands to be able to tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please refer to the entry of your diary of the 14th of July 1992. And you referred -- first of all, this says basically the decision of the war presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka to dismiss the main editor of Glas, Mladjenovic, article, "Art for fighters, fighters for art," petition to replace Kupresanin and Brdjanin, with some statements, allegedly police have information on perpetrators -- that's not important. Source unknown, et cetera. You testified on this at some length here. And amongst other things, you mentioned that you had spoken to Mladjenovic, the editor of Glas. And you told us that you wanted to encourage him in his fight against the triumvirate Radoslav Brdjanin, Kupresanin, Vukic. Now, why would you even dream of encouraging Mladjenovic of such a thing if he was the editor, until then, of Glas, of a newspaper which you compare with Goebbels' Beobachter? Why would you have anything to do with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. This was a Machiavellian approach, if you will, where the ends justify the means. I knew that the moment they start confronting each other, their dirty laundry will come into light, if you understand. Miro advocated one faction, and they were another. Miro Mladjenovic was great friends with Borivoje Sendic, Veljko Milankovic, an Orthodox criminal who had at least 180 criminal reports brought against him before they were liquidated -- before he was liquidated by Serbs themselves because he was in some fuel business and he was a nuisance to Mladic himself. So Miro was on one side, and the others were on the other. Even Vojo Kupresanin, in some moments of sincerity, that 70 per cent of Serbian soldiers were simply looters, robbers. So this was his honest statement. My idea was, and I was doing this for private reasons, not on behalf of anyone, I wanted to encourage him, because I knew he was a coward, and I hoped that whatever he knew of the others that was negative, that he would come out with it. Because you have to know that there was a series in the papers where he was talking about Brane Palackovic, who was an untouchable personality in Banja Luka, and allegedly he had committed 90 crimes ever since the inception of the SOS. He was beating up people, robbing, looting, and only after we had read this in the paper did we learn about Palackovic. And previously, Glas would not write about this. So I wanted to encourage him, although as you noticed I did not introduce myself. I just said that I was a friend of his brother's, which I was. I wanted them to fight each other in order to come out with the truth, for the people to learn the truth. I was far from thinking that I was going to solve the situation, but I simply wanted to heat up the friction that existed among them. And I assure you that this did yield results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Without speculating, could you tell us what was the reason behind the pressure that was exerted, that was put on Mladjenovic and which ended up with his removal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the reason. Well, Mladjenovic is a very vain person. He was initially minister for information. Then they released him, and he was then an escort to Prince Karadjordjevic, which meant a lot to him. And then suddenly he was marginalised by the top leadership which either made him envious or he simply could not cope with the fact that he had been pushed into the background. He then started placing obstacles to them, started making problems to them, and that's when their quarrel became an open one. So despite the fact that they were saying that they were advocating the interests of the Serbs, they were basically following their private interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did his support to Veljko Milankovic have anything to do with the pressure to have him removed, to your knowledge? I don't want you to speculate. You either know or you don't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain, but I do think that this could have had something to do with it, because he was almost a saint there, defending Serbian people. But then when they started investigating him, they found that he had some 100 cars over there which he had stolen. He was a criminal, stealing jewellery and so on. Miro liked having such a player at his side, and this probably served as a deterrent to the other side which, since Miro had such a person by him, they probably -- the other side probably didn't feel as secure because a criminal is a criminal. He has no ideals, but you know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want you to put in front of you a vision of Glas before the removal of Mladjenovic, and Glas post-removal of Mladjenovic. Did the editorial policy of Glas change, visible change, after his removal? Or did it remain the same or was there no significant change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all remained the same. Miro Mladjenovic actually was a person behind Glas. Anyway, he was formally removed, but he did dictate the editorial policy, but backstage, so to speak. He wasn't responsible any more, but all the journalists continued supporting him. They all belonged to the same -- they all frequented the same school. Glas did stand out in a way. Miro was removed, but the policy remained absolutely the same. Yesterday, we were reading Glas when he was the main editor, and then if you look at Glas after he had been removed you can see that he was he still the one pulling the strings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was there any other editor of any other newspaper or radio station or TV station that was dealt with in the same manner? In other words, that was forced out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were removals in the Banja Luka Radio. I cannot recall them at present. I cannot remember anything specifically, but I do know that there were one, two, or maybe even three putsches within the Banja Luka Radio when people were saying that they were being forcefully removed. Banja Luka Radio even broadcast this openly. I did write this down in my diary, but there were such removals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did they occur more or less around the same time that Mladjenovic was removed from editor of Glas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, on the 4th of August you have an entry in your diary which refers to the red van. Now, we've heard a lot about this red van. And you also give the registration number of this red van. Did the existing -- existence of this red van and the use it was being made of receive any publicity in the media? Did anyone speak about it, write about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not at all, at least not as far as I know. And believe me, I looked at all the newspapers I could lay my hands on very carefully. He was never mentioned in any of the media. This was simply something that was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us why there was no reference in the papers or in the media to something that we've heard so much about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not mentioned only so that one day you could not get hold of one of those newspapers and see what this all about. You, or somebody else who would be astonished to read about it. The red van was part of their policy of intimidation and making life difficult for people of other ethnic backgrounds. They were not foolish enough to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Who was behind this policy? Army? Civilian authorities? Private citizens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. They were all the same team. What army? When a man like Kupresanin can say about the JNA, which was the fourth largest force in Europe, to say they cannot take a single bullet out of Banja Luka, how could these Serbs have stopped them, had they not all been part of the same team, playing the same game? This was thought up somewhere at the top, and who was the strongest player, whether the army or General Uzelac or Kupresanin or Brdjanin or Vukic at any given moment, it's hard for us to say. It was a fact, however, when that van and many other things people know about, when this red van drove through the town, people's blood froze in their veins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you describe those men in the van as armed men in camouflage uniform. So having a uniform at that time doesn't mean anything? It doesn't automatically mean they belong to the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: What yes? Can you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't mean anything. The Serbs started arming in early 1992. They were already all armed. Even children had hand grenades. Suddenly camouflage uniforms appeared -- well, first, there were olive-grey uniforms, followed by camouflage uniforms, and it was a question of prestige. There was a joke going around Banja Luka, how will you recognise Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka? And the answer was: Well, they're wearing civilian clothes. They were all dressed like Rambo. And there was no way you can know whether they were members of regular units or paramilitary units or whether it was simply a group of criminals that had got together, put on uniforms and made life difficult for the citizens. But you were not allowed to ask. You had no rights. Anyone could stop you, ask to see whether you'd been mobilised or ask you anything, and beat you up. You had no rights. Who would you call? The police? They wouldn't protect you. The police would not protect you against their own, their brother Serbs. That's how it was, unfortunately. The uniform meant nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So what would be your answer if I put to you in your opinion, experience, what you heard from others, wasn't there any force possibility to stop those people, by the police, by the army, by the civilian authorities? Was it possible to do that? Can you state that? If there would be the will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible. For example, the incident we mentioned last time, the shootout between Vedran Mandic, and Kajkut Mihajlovic, the attack on the Mejdan police station when they were fighting about dividing up the loot and the police liquidated the criminals. These criminals had long criminal records and yet the police had protected them up to that moment, cooperated with them. However, then they fell out over dividing the booty. The police could have dealt with them if they wanted to, but the police was as unreliable as the criminals were. I said that the commander of the Majdan police station raped several Muslim and Croat women, and I saw Mr. Brdjanin waving this off. He was replaced the following year, but not before -- not because he raped those women; it was because he killed a man, and this man was a Serb policeman who stopped him at a checkpoint. He took out his pistol and shot him, although it was one of his own policeman who was standing there and had to stop him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: How did you see Mr. Brdjanin just wave his hand on it? Can you describe the situation a little bit? You saw it or you heard it? Can you be clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this looking at the video of my previous testimony. When I said that the police commander had raped a few women, he waved his hand in a resigned way. I allow that Brdjanin may not have known about this. This commander's name was Petar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And people were terrified of him. He would go around the checkpoints toward Vrbani and Celinac to make sure people couldn't get out and that they felt insecure and that they couldn't get food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the commander's name? It was Petar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Tanazic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Judge Janu. Could I refer you now, please, to your entry for the 11th August 1992. I have a series of questions on this entry. Let's start from the beginning of this entry. (Redacted) (Redacted) Did he describe it to you or did he describe it to someone else and you got to know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she told me about this personally. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And she was horrified (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one of the things you mention is the freedom of 18 movement for Muslims in Celinac is restricted to four hours a day. (Redacted) 19 (Redacted) But in your testimony, you mention about a law, laws that prevented Muslims from moving around in Celinac. Are you sure there were laws in place that had been put in place restricting the freedom of movement of Muslims in Celinac, or is this existence of laws something on which you're not precise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am absolutely sure of one thing. I don't know whether the law was written down, but I know that people followed it. And it was not only to do with Celinac, Your Honour. I was not allowed to move around Banja Luka unless I had a certificate stating that I had regulated my mobilisation duties because there had been a general call-up. I don't know whether this was actually written down as law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to know the following. You say that the situation in the town is probably the result of the policy of the former president of Celinac Municipality, Radoslav Brdjanin. Is this your own conclusion, (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had thought about this. Do you have any concerns about the name of this lady being mentioned in open session, or shall we play it cautious and redact it? I'm asking both you and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought you were asking the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am asking you. Maybe you know this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never heard of her. Other than through the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think once we have mentioned this person's name, she would require some kind of protection? We strike her name off from the transmission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, yes, I would like that to be done. I know where she lives and what the consequences of what I have said might be, although I'm sure she would abide by what I've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we will redact her name wherever it appears in the transcript. Then again, at the same entry, in the same entry, you continue as follows: "At the question of one of his colleagues of what to do with mixed marriage children, Brdjanin reportedly said, 'we will throw them into the Vrbas, the ones who resurface are definitely Serbs.'" How did you come across this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the people who were there told me about this. I have to say I didn't hear it personally. And I know that some people from the town laughed at this and said this is a mistake. In the town, there is the River Vrbas, and two or three other rivers, and we all knew how to swim. And it was least of all the Serbs who knew how to swim because they lived up in the hills. And we lived near the river. So if someone drowned, it would most probably have been a Serb. That was the interpretation of the people who laughed when they commented on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this was not something that this woman told you, together with the rest of the information --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, further down in the same entry, you state: "HTV." What's HTV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. "HTV programme, Slikom Na Sliku is devoted to concentration camps." Now, can you give us more information on this. First of all, was this -- could you receive this station in Banja Luka? How did you come to know about this HTV programme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, it was still possible to see. You couldn't see the image very well. There was like snow on the screen, but you could see a bit. And we all wanted to peer over the fence to see what the other people were saying. There were times when we could see and times when we couldn't. However, after -- at a later date, the picture disappeared and all we could follow was the broadcast from Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your testimony is that when you say HTV programme, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, it's because you saw it? You watched this programme on TV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I did. I managed to see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which concentration camps did it refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably about Omarska, perhaps Manjaca. This was a frequent topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recall ever having seen Mr. Brdjanin or having heard Mr. Brdjanin deal with the topic of these camps, of camps in general or in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't recall Mr. Brdjanin being interviewed on TV, for example, on these camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. On one occasion, I think he said on television -- no, I don't think. I'm sure he said on one occasion: "If the Russians and the Germans could have camps, why shouldn't we, the Serbs, be able to have camps?" I think the broadcast was called Otvoreni Ekran or something like that. I think I heard that on just one occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to hear Mr. Ostojic speak on the camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He kept saying that the Serbs didn't have camps, that they were only prisons. And at one point, he attacked Glas saying that Glas was writing all sorts of things. He was even against Miro Mladjenovic. He said that Glas was writing about nonsense and that Reuters discovered the camps because of them. Then he kind of mitigated this by saying: "We have nothing to hide, but don't write all sorts of things."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the same entry, however, you said -- you referred to one interview or one statement by Ostojic who seems, at least to the -- according to the translation that I have here, to be saying exactly the opposite. According to your entry, Ostojic said that "some things are better left unsaid, not because they have to stay hidden." Was he referring to the camps when he said these, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it says. If you will allow me: "Minister Ostojic went on to say that some things should not be written about, not because there was something to hide, but because it was not politically the right time, saying that the journalist of the Reuters agency had found a news item in the Glas about the transfer of prisoners of war from Trnopolje to Manjaca. When the camp was discovered, they rounded up these people, took them off to Manjaca, and then said, "you see, we've released them." He was, in fact, criticising Glas for writing about this and, thus, allowing Reuters to find out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recall any articles or any programmes on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. camps in 1992, in any of the papers or on any of the media, TV or radio stations? Was it something that was being discussed, or was it something that was being put aside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, as I understand it, to discuss is one thing and to publish is another. Nothing was published. If we talk about the Serbian side in Banja Luka, there was no talk of camps. We all knew, however, that camps existed. My next-door neighbour was a camp guard in Manjaca. He told me such terrible things that at first I was unable to believe him. Afterwards, I got to know some doctors who were up there and who told me certain things. These people were kept in stables, stables where you had room for 60 cows on one side and 60 cows on another were packed with 800 people. They called this a prison. There were children there, elderly people when the international community discovered this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard enough about Manjaca and Omarska and the rest, but what I want to know is whether you recall having read anything or heard anything in the papers or on TV? Nothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only read that the Serbs had no camps, that they had only prisons and centres. It's interesting to note, however, that when the international community arrived, people would take people from the prison and send them off to mosques. And people went there bringing bread and food to these unfortunate people. They put them in mosques and mosque courtyards. And even Muslim doctors said "don't take them so much food. You'll kill them. They have been starving, and if they eat all that food suddenly, they may die."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. May I refer you to your entry of the 28th of August. I'm sorry, I didn't tell you about this yesterday, but I thought about it today. You have a very short entry there. First of all, you state that Glas was not published that day, was not printed due to lack of paper. And then you say: "A man from Brdjanin's security says Brdjanin is under great pressure." Now, what are you talking about? Where did you get this information and what is this great pressure that this Brdjanin security man seems to be referring to? 28th of August, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking for it. Oh, yes. You mean this, I also learned from the people that this -- it says here: "Milorad Brdjanin is often caught in the fire and as soon as he gets angry at the people he receives, he throws things at them. And says come and sit where I am sitting." Yes, this is Brdjanin, and the name Milorad is here by mistake. Well, he was certainly under tremendous pressure. Whether we wish to admit this or not, that's how it was. His village, the people in the village where he was born, from Popovac, they kept coming to see him and asking him for this and that, saying, "Well, now we've got the state, do this and that for me." And of course he was nervous. He was besieged by people asking him for favours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Great pressure can mean more than one thing, so you gave us the context in which you wrote it down. So more or less you're talking of stress. More or less you're talking of stress, and not pressure by other people on him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean any particular side. I just think he wasn't having an easy time. He certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I mentioned this to you yesterday. You mentioned in your testimony at page 18.010 of the transcript about the man who got beaten when you brought them to a doctor and whose picture became Exhibit P2325. If it's necessary, I'll show you the picture, but I think you will remember who we are talking about. What was the ethnicity, what was the nationality of this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I recall this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was his nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why he was beaten up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what he told me. In fact, I was going to see a friend of mine to have a cup of coffee with him. And he told me that a man who had been beaten up was lying in his workshop. This was a man who was repairing body -- a car body -- bodies. And he -- actually, he wasn't the one working there, but he had keys to the workshop. So when I went there and saw that the man had been beaten black and blue, I told my friend to just try and see whether he had fever, and I said I was going to get a doctor. So I did find a doctor who dressed his wounds as far as he could, provided first aid to him because he was bleeding, he was vomiting blood. He was a man by the name of Sejo Pucar. He lived at Odica Street [phoen]. And he recounted me. He told me everything about the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any reports on this incident in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. At least 20 or 30 people were being beaten up every night, and where would they end up if they reported on each and every one of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do I read you clear that, in fact, you're telling us that no reports ever appeared in the media on this or similar incidents? Because if you're saying that there were 30 such incidents a day ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately. That was my estimate. In the papers and on the TV, you could hear a report by the public security station saying that in the course of the previous night, some 15 burglaries were recorded, and someone committed suicide, something was broken into, a bomb was thrown or something. But if someone had been beaten up, you would hear no reports about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, can I refer to your entries -- entry of the 5th of April of 1992. And we are going to deal very briefly with the SOS. Before we do so, Judge Janu has got one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I would like to go back to this so-called Mr. Brdjanin's pronouncement concerning the swimming test for the children. Can you tell me -- you say here "reportedly." Can you tell me how long do you know Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, ever since he had entered politics I was able to see him. But I do not know him personally. I know him -- that is, I know his elderly daughter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My best friend was a teacher of hers in the high school. That is what I know about Brdjanin, in addition to what I heard from the people, from the papers that I read, his statements, from what I heard on the TV and then typed it down. I do not know Mr. Brdjanin personally, nor had I heard of him prior to all these events started unfolding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And this lady - I will not mention her name - that nurse who gave you some informations, she knew him well, living -- being from Celinac? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Did she know him personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot claim either way now. But I think not. Celinac being a small town, she saw him frequently. Probably when she was at work, they would come across each other. But it is difficult for me to say whether they knew each other personally. I may have written something down about it, but I cannot tell you anything of my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So you cannot say that "because I know Mr. Brdjanin so well, so I believe it's probable that he used those words about this test for children"? You cannot say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the people who had told me so because these were very serious people to say something. These were professors, doctors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: No, no, no. I want to know from your own experience, knowledge of his character and all this, that you believe this could be given to assume to him? It wasn't a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of all of his statements, I do believe so. However, I have to underline the fact that I did not hear him say so. I've heard it from people who I trust, and I believe that this was indeed true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you standing, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour: Page 23, line 23, that the translator missed. What he said was "his daughter Milka, who is really a wonderful girl."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, this goes into page 23 -- I was looking at 22. 23, yes. Okay, thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Do you confirm that? Do you confirm having said what Mr. Ackerman has just mentioned; namely, that you had also said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What, that I said Milka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Milja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's Mr. Ackerman is obsessed with the...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said Milja, and Mr. Ackerman said Milka. So his mind is still there. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Any further remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I hope there's no confusion, Your Honour, about this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness said with regard to Mr. Brdjanin's statement about swimming in the Vrbas River, that it was not the woman he talked to from Celinac who told him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is clear. That's why I put the question in any case, because I wanted to make clear whether this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure there was no confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and while we are still in time, you mentioned the name and surname of the Muslim man who was attacked and that you then took to the doctor. Shall we redact his name? Is he still alive? If we leave his --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can leave his name. I hope that he is alive. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Yes, let me take you to the 5th of April and the previous two days. We're dealing with the SOS. And on the 5th of April, after that the Crisis Staff had been formed, you have -- you make an entry. You enter in your diary that Brdjanin is making statements on the SOS demands and the acceptance by the Crisis Staff. Can you go into more details, because it seems that the ones who spoke about this was Vukic and Brdjanin on that occasion, at least according to your entry. What did Brdjanin actually say that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he supported these men on the barricades who were asking for the war profiteers to be removed. In April when the Serbian Defence Forces appeared, the entire town was swarming with armed men. We didn't know where they had come from. They walked around. They would stop everyone, mistreat people. They would pull over buses. And whenever they came across a Croat or a Muslim, they would take jewellery off them, kick them off the bus. So they would be mistreating them in all different ways. And we simply thought this was some sort of a gang that went out of hand. We never even thought that the state, whichever state it was, that it was not going to intervene. At one point, the Banja Luka Radio started broadcasting the announcement of the Serbian Defence Forces, that they had placed some -- put forward some conditions that they are protecting combatants on the front, and you know, they're talking about protecting those on the front and they're in the town. So they put forward some ten conditions, and they asked that sort of a board be established that would represent their interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What my question was, what do you recall Mr. Brdjanin --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Brdjanin was supposed to be a member of this body. And since he always wanted to be a high-profile man, he was turned into the spokesman of this group that would meet. And out of the ten demands that the group had presented previously, they adopted 11. I believe that they had forgotten what the SOS had been asking for, and then they simply adopted their decisions. So the levelling of the cadres, one of the demands was for the ethnic composition to be completely changed. We were talking -- maybe this was yesterday or during my previous testimony, there were two Muslims who were directors of the Metal company. So why couldn't they be directors? Simply because they were Muslims. So if I'm a Serb, but not an intelligent person, why would I be more suitable to occupy a post than someone else and so on? It was then basically that the putsch took place. That was the time that the takeover took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And go to 14th June 1992, please. We are soon finished.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As the saying goes: "Those who will walk behind me will be" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it has been interpreted. I apologise. I haven't had a smoke in a long time. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should quit. Yes. Did you go to the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are quoted there, you are saying Vukic encouraging or saying that -- on TV that Serbian radio and TV should engage in a stronger propaganda in favour of the Serb force. Was he drunk when he said this, or was he sober?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was very difficult to find him sober. Whether he was a bit more inebriated or a bit less, that's difficult for me to say. Because his intoxication had different degrees. He would say many different things. You said the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: June. June.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: June, no, I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. Forget it. We're moving forward with another question. Judge Janu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to put you a few questions which are of more general character. I would like to know some of your opinions. The first one, what's your opinion about Mr. Tudjman and his contribution to the tension and later conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion of him cannot be more negative than it is. He's conceited, uneducated. I think that he was the great misfortune of the Croatian people because with his mad policy, it was him who had caused the conflict between Muslims and Croats. I don't have a good opinion of him. And if I may say, in 1992, I was writing in the Croatian press against him and his policy vis-a-vis Bosnia. I think that he was -- he was disastrous for Bosnian Croats because of his alliance with Milosevic on the issue of the division of Bosnia. And that is what I can say about the late President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation why he was re-elected as a president in the situation where there was more or less democracy in the country, or at least the free elections? Do you have any explanation for this behaviour of the majority of Croatian people? If you have; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very difficult question. I believe he had indebted many people. You know that Croatia as a country had been practically sold out to many people. He was perhaps even afraid that he was going to be held to account for the privatisation which was carried out irregularly, and many people profited from it. So maybe some of these who had profited from it were for him. But it's difficult to say. One cannot predict what people will do. Serbs had a wonderful politician, Nikola Pasic, a radical, who spoke of the people as follows: "People, you are my strength; people, you are cattle."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. And another question: What's your opinion about Mr. Izetbegovic's Islamic Declaration which was reprinted in 1990? And again, concerning its influence on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, if any influence. If you are able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour. This declaration has to be read out -- read in its entirety because you know what happens when things get pulled out of the context. I believe that the declaration did not have any impact on anything. It wasn't fatal in any sense. In Banja Luka, I had far more Serb and Muslim friends than Croats. I only maybe had two friends among the Croats. And I know that it was Muslims, Bosniaks who were least passionate about the national issue. And maybe it was precisely because of their - how to call it even - that they are perhaps to blame for my Banja Luka, for what happened in my Banja Luka because when the elections were held, Serbs voted for Serbs, the SDS, and Croats for the HDZ. And the Muslims divided their votes, for the SDA, for Nijaz Durakovic's party, for Izetbegovic's SDA, for Ante Markovic and his reformist forces, then the Yugoslav-oriented parties. Their votes were divided. Had they really stood by the Declaration as someone is trying to present, then they would have won. I don't think the Declaration had a role to play. If you take a look at my diary and if you pull some things out of the context, then it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. And if you -- what would you tell us about Mr. Izetbegovic himself in comparison what you said with -- about Franjo Tudjman and maybe in comparison with Mr. Milosevic? If you can be very concise, I would be happy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija was a man who was most reticent. He was a believer, the only one of the three. And I believe that he had to play to the tune of the other two. He had a country with three nations, where two nations were raising their hand against the others. Serbs were saying that they had their country proper, Serbia; Croats are Croatia; and Muslims had only Bosnia. And poor things, they had to somehow try and survive between these two sides. In any case, he should not be regarded as having taken either side or as being responsible for these -- some of the fatal things that happened for Bosnia. He, perhaps, made some mistakes. Certainly, he did make some mistakes. But he is far, far less -- the things that he could do were zero in comparison to what the other two persons could do, and they were the ones who dictated all the events and the developments that we experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So in your opinion, he's an honest man, or he was an honest man? Because he's not living any more.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Even if he had been the worst of persons, there was little that he could do. The possibilities were few. He wasn't a bad person. I don't think so. Perhaps he just made some bad moves. But he couldn't do much. He had to weigh things all the time, and in weighing things, he might have made some wrong moves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You said he was a believer. What did you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Believer? He believed in God, in Islam? And what was the -- yeah, just this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, a believer is a person who believes in God, regardless of whether he is a Christian or a Muslim. Anyway, religion is in a way out of joint with politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And the conflict in Bosnia is sometimes from outside viewed as a conflict of religions. What's your opinion, of these three religions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. What is my opinion of this? I think that this is a great tragedy, and if there is God -- and anyway, every religion says "don't kill, don't steal." The ones to blame are the religious communities. They committed as many mistakes as the media did. So these religious communities are also to blame for what had happened. Take a look at Bosnia today. In the Croatian part, you have churches -- the church is outspoken. In the other part, Muslim part, Islam is very loud. So even if you don't have any money to build hospitals or universities, you will always have enough money to build a church or a mosque. And this speaks for everything really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So what was the role of orthodox church, or other churches, all churches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the most horrible role was the one played by the Orthodox church. I recall in -- it was in 1992 in Belgradsko Vreme where the photograph was published of a priest wearing, holding a submachine-gun, and I think that would tell you everything. I don't know what Catholic priests, on the other hand, were like simply because I'm not a practicing believer. I don't go to church. But I believe that there were extremists among them as well. I know that there are such extremists even today in Croatia. What the situation is like with the Muslims, I cannot say. In Banja Luka, when I was there, an honourable man lived there, a Banja Luka Muftija. Unfortunately, he died. Efendi Ibrahim Halilovic. He was a wonderful man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: What about the name Bishop Jevtic? Do you know that name, Jevtic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: What about another name, Bishop, if I'm right, Filaret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Filaret, yes, that was the one I was telling you about. He was taken a picture holding a machine-gun. He was a hawk. Amfilohije Radovic as well. It doesn't even cross my mind to condemn the church as an institution. However, I believe that this time some of the clerics who betrayed the religion, the God, and the people, that they should be prosecuted as well. And in addition to them, even the representatives of the media who contributed to the spreading of hatred and who contributed to bringing about all these developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Was there any reflection of guilt in the Orthodox church after the war? Did you -- could you hear something or see or read? Did the church itself -- has the church itself done something about the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I think that experts should be consulted on these matters, experts who had followed the situation. It is very difficult for me to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't want to keep the staff unduly here. We'll have a 25-minute break. And then we will proceed, but we'll soon finish. How much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what the end result was. Do I go first or Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We agreed yesterday you go first, and then Mr. Ackerman goes last. And then you hoped ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I'll probably be about three-quarters of an hour to an hour. I don't know how many more questions Your Honour has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're practically finished. And you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About the same, Your Honour, maybe a little less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we should finish by the end of the next session, roughly, more or less. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, before we proceed with the testimony of the witness, Ms. Korner -- Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the testimony of the witness, you filed a motion confidentially for the protective measures for your witness in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being -- do you have anything to say with regard to that, Mr. Ackerman? No. We have given it due consideration. Our decision is to grant the motion with the caveat regarding whether the witness should testify in closed session or not. If it's the case, we will interview the witness in the beginning and then we will decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But otherwise, the protective measures requested are being granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Janu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Witness, that as a journalist you are familiar with the expression "verbal symbolism" as a form of expression. I would like to know, going back to your statement that there was these four horsemen of apocalypse, Kupresanin, Vukic, Radic, and Mr. Brdjanin, Who do you think, if you know, was using this type of expression, verbal symbolism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think all of them, all four of them actually did. I think it was all four of them. Some of them to a larger extent; others to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question: Maybe you told us, but I don't remember. I don't recall. Were you -- before the war, during this difficult in Bosnia, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never was I a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So am I right, you were not a member of the League of Communists as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Janu. Judge Taya from Japan would like to put some questions to you, sir. Judge Taya.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: During 1992, out of politician, who appeared very often in Belgrade TV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the politicians who were carving our fate in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or are you referring to Yugoslav politicians in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Yugoslav ones were concerned, Milosevic was there every day. I think he appeared most often out of all politicians. Then our politicians from Krajina would get their turn once all the trouble started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Among those politicians, who was the most detrimental to the ethnic tension in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the politicians from Bosnia was Radovan Karadzic, no doubt. After him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the Belgrade TV.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Milosevic for sure. Then Dobrica Cosic and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I want to know the same question, the same point about the Pale TV.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: TV Pale, well, I can tell you one thing. Whoever appeared there was working against Bosnia and to the detriment of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Who appeared very often on TV Pale during 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Ostojic, Buha, Maksimovic, they appeared the most often. Those are the faces we saw most of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Among these politicians, who was the most detrimental to incite the ethnic tension in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic, no doubt. Then, say, Krajisnik, then Ostojic. These are terrible people. Buha, Maksimovic, all of them were -- well, it's very hard to say. It's a question of nuance. But I think that Karadzic is on the very top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the time being, we don't have any further questions from our side. Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I want to go back to something that you were asked about yesterday. This is at page 28 of the LiveNote. And you were being asked about the difference between town and rural population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said this, and I think there may have been an error. I noticed it at the time, in the transcript. You said there was another characteristic of Bosnia which was quite important, especially in cases of villages where only one nationality lived. And then what's been written is: "It was very difficult to delude the people. This was often done by local priests who frequently played rather dishonourable roles in our society." Did you mean it was difficult to delude people or easy to delude people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was easy to delude people, because -- I mean, these clergymen there, they were in such positions of importance that they could actually abuse what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. I thought it didn't otherwise make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, I want to deal with something you raised. Sorry. This was to do with the Serbian academy of arts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he raised it at page 39. The SANU memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember that? Just answer yes or no, because then I'm going to show you the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've now got that memorandum, and I'd like to hand it out to Your Honours. A copy for the witness, and then I'm just going to ask him to look at one part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would question the basis upon what it's being used for at this point. It has been a subject of this case from the very beginning, and the Prosecution having rested their case should not be able to just put documents into evidence any longer because they feel like it. I don't think it responds to anything this witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not aware it has been the subject of any discussion other than in passing in Professor Donia's -- I'm now doing this. Dr. Donia's testimony. At page 40 of the LiveNote yesterday, Judge Janu said -- asked him: "Sir, you were telling us about the involvement of academics from the academy of sciences. Do you remember some names, some leading personalities?" In those circumstances, it's our submission we are entitled to put the document in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think so, yes. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just say for the record I think that would require an application to reopen the case because all that was asked about was the names, and he gave the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question of the society was brought up, and let's see what the question is anyway. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've made my objection. I'm just making the record. That's what I'm doing, and I think I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can be given a copy, please, sir. And I just want you to -- is this -- this is -- it was -- I think the situation as we have been told, it was leaked to the press, and then it was thereafter published in various sources. This is one published in Zagreb. But is this what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All I want to -- you said this was really the beginnings of the propaganda. Could you go, please, to -- I did mark the page. What page did I say it was? It's the second-to-the-last page, page 161. In the translation, Your Honours, it's page 335.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see there it's the paragraph that begins: "It is the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. historical and democratic right of the Serbian People to establish their full national and cultural integrity" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, I can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then jumping the next sentence, "gain equality and independent development has a deep historical meaning for the Serbian nation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What page are we on in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In less than 50 years, through two successive generations, twice exposed to physical destruction, forced assimilation, christening, cultural genocide, ideological indoctrination, underestimation, renouncement of their own tradition under the imposed feeling of guilt, intellectually and politically disarmed," and so on and so forth. And then it says: "If it sees its future in the family of cultural and civilised nations of the world, Serbian nation must gain the opportunity to find itself and become a historical subject. To regain awareness of its historical and spiritual being, to clearly define its economic and cultural interests." And then going right down, please, to the bottom of the page: "The biggest trouble - this is the third sentence - the biggest trouble is the Serbian People do not have a state, whilst all the other nations do." Now, sir, did you read this memorandum or excerpts from it at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time it was not actually being made public. It went from hand to hand, so I managed to see some excerpts from the memorandum. But these were some kind of secret sessions that were held. That's what it seemed like to me, at any rate, where these people who made these decisions, these academicians, these people at the Writers' Club in Belgrade, the address being Francuska Street number 7, they discussed it, they debated it. At the same time, this was being written about increasingly in the press, that Serbia was being exploited by the other republics and also in the Politika daily, there was this amazing section called "Reverberations and Reactions," and the idea being promoted there was that everything was being taken away from Serbia and it was being exploited. So it was just preparation of what was to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you also said yesterday, you were being asked questions by Judge Agius at that stage, and that is at page 36 of the LiveNote. And you were asked: "Do you mean to tell us, because this means" -- 37, sorry. "This needs to be clear, that in your mind the media were not calling for genocide but were creating an atmosphere which led to genocide." I would just like you to tell the Court, please, sir, what you mean when you use the word "genocide."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say "genocide," I mean eradication, making a nation extinct, destroying its places of worship. What is genocide for me? Let me explain it in the most practical possible way. In Banja Luka towards the end of the 19th century, there were 41 mosques, for instance. Nowadays, there is no trace of a mosque. A state cannot be built on destroyed cemeteries and places of worship. That is genocide for me. Cultural genocide, too. Many people were killed as well. So that's what I mean by it. I don't know if I was precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. We just wanted to know so we're all clear on what you meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, incidentally with regard to the previous question and the reason why we admitted the document that Ms. Korner made use of, Mr. Ackerman, please refer to yesterday's transcript, page 40, line 17. The witness is answering when he was asked for the names by Judge Janu. He said: "Of course, I do. The entire academy of arts and sciences, the Belgrade-based academy of arts and sciences, first, they published the memorandum, the infamous memorandum, and then a number of the members, Cosic and others, they were all working on the same agenda. They wanted to appear..." And it goes on and on and on. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think this could be admitted without someone certifying or telling you that this is actually the memorandum. If you'll notice, it is -- it's contained in a thing called: "Roots of Serbian aggression" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- that is published in Zagreb and apparently authored by some people in Zagreb. And it may very well just be propaganda. And so I worry about it from that standpoint. I can't say it's not the memorandum, but I can't say it is. It could very well just be Croat propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And certainly, if it's going to come in, that page that says "Roots of Serbian aggression" does not belong there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you look, it's an English translation. But in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We also have the B/C/S one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The B/C/S doesn't have that. It's the simplest way of getting the translation. In any event, let's not argue this out, please. Your Honours have admitted it. Mr. Ackerman has made his objection. There's another translation of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One is enough, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. I forgot to ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still don't have an exhibit number. I see Mr. Ackerman standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make it very clear that the B/C/S version is also from Zagreb, and I'll check -- I'll check my real copy when I get home tonight. This may very well just be a propaganda piece. It may not be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I invite you, Mr. Ackerman, to check your own personal copy of this gripping document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2730, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked a number of questions about Mr. Brdjanin's appearances on Radio Banja Luka and on TV Banja Luka. And you said at page 45: "He spoke on the radio constantly." And then at page 46, you were asked about TV Banja Luka. And you say: "I rely mostly on my diary, but he did appear very often." Could you have, please, your diary for May, starting with the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in the middle of our translation, the first part of the entry, you say - and this is the programme you referred to yesterday as well; you called it "Open Screen" - is that the same one that we can see referred to there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is a radio programme called "Uvika Otvorena," [phoen] Radio Banja Luka. This is a radio show, whereas the other one is a TV show.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Quite right. Anyhow, you say: "On this programme, on the 5th of May we had the opportunity to hear from the mastermind behind all this madness, Radoslav Brdjanin, who was invited to clear up some things for the listeners of Radio Banja Luka." Then you talk about the interview. "The man openly showed that he will risk absolutely everything, and thousands of young lives for a sick dream of a state." Then he talks about the Philippines air force, and then he says: "He only wants one thing. He will not give up power at any cost. For the first time, a Brdjanin has a chance to enter into history and for the first time he can do anything he wants." And you go on to give examples. Now, two things, please, sir. First, trying to put yourself back into that day in May of 1992, what made you write the words "we had the opportunity to hear from the mastermind behind all this madness"? What was it that made you say in May of 1992, he was the mastermind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could hardly be put that way, that Radoslav Brdjanin was the mastermind, that he conceived of all of this. He was one of the creators of this self-defeating policy. This had to do with mobilisation, as far as I could see now, rapidly as I glanced at it. He stood behind this self-defeating policy. He was a prominent proponent of this policy. Now, what made me say this? Everything he said in the media showed that this was a man who did not hesitate to use big words, and big words lead to big consequences. He labelled other ethnic groups, glorified his own. All of that was sufficient reason for me to view him the way I did and to assess him the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, you don't say -- this is what I'm trying to see. I know it's difficult 11, 12 years on to cast yourself back into the atmosphere of the times. But you say Brdjanin was the mastermind, not one of the masterminds, but the mastermind. Can you now recall what it was about him that made you label him that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has already answered that. He said "It could hardly be put that way, that Brdjanin was the mastermind, that he conceived of all this." He has already answered it. It is being asked the same way again, and she is likely to get the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That may be so, but I'm entitled to ask the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a difference, Mr. Ackerman. That's his position now, today. What he's being asked to answer is then, 12 years ago, when he wrote -- described Radoslav Brdjanin as the mastermind. Why did he then describe him so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the same question. Look at line 19:44. Put yourself back on that day in May 1992, what made you write the words? Why can she ask it twice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the same question, I agree with you, but it's not the same answer. Because he answered the question from the present perspective, today's perspective. He's answering the question with hindsight. What he's being asked is to go back in time to 12 years ago, remember that this is what he wrote, and he is being asked to explain why he described Brdjanin as the mastermind then, not why he thinks whether he now believes -- still believes that he was the mastermind. He told us already that he doesn't believe he was the mastermind with hindsight. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can't now, if you can't recall what it was that made you say that in 1992, then say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall what made me say that in that year. It was everything he said in public, all his inflammatory speeches after which terrible things happened.
