When buildings belonging to members of other ethnic groups were blown up, all of that led me to write this, that he was guilty of that. No doubt about it. That is why I said that he was some kind of a mastermind and bigtime troublemaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You see, you were asked a number of questions, and I am looking now at page 48, about the quote that he decided on life and death. And you then said: "I'm not saying he really wanted bad things to happen to Croats and Muslims. I don't want to say that, but the way he addressed himself, the way he spoke, and his public announcements in the mass media, the way he spoke, he caused panic among the people. That's what he did, and that's a fact." And you went on to explain that. And in the end, you said in your view, he used the mass media as an instrument for his own advancement. And that's page 52. Now, how was he going to obtain his own advancement, as far as you could see, through the things that you've described, the terrible things that he was saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how I could see it. One has to know all the people in Bosnia, especially the ethnic group that Mr. Brdjanin belongs to. Among the Serbs, it is their folk poetry, their verses that matter the most. By what he did, he became part of this poetry, and that was so important. You have the most telling example here of Mr. Milosevic. Everybody knows what this is all about. He's no fool either, but he is struggling for his place in history. So that's it. That's what Mr. Brdjanin wanted, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether he personally disliked Muslims and Croats or privately liked them, despite what he was saying in public, did that in your view make any difference to the way that his utterances in public were regarded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An interesting question. I think this will surprise you. Many of my friends told me that Mr. Brdjanin often visited a hodza in Vrbanja, Jasarevic. He would go there rather often to have a cup of coffee with him. As I said, when he was in a good mood, he would often say: "My friends, Muslims." And indeed, this was so and cannot be denied. In some of his speeches, he gave the impression of a very sober man, but it was as if the fact that he had taken the floor, that he would talk to the microphone, that he would change. Monologues would flow out of his mouth, and everything that he said could have served to those who wanted to settle accounts with the heathens, the pagans, as he sometimes put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the fact that it might have been known to some people that he did visit a hodza or have Muslim friends, did that make his threats any less, as you've told, it likely to cause panic and terror?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In essence, you had a very peculiar situation. Every Serb in Banja Luka had his own Muslim or Croat. Because the Serb was aware of the fact that some of the bad things are going to happen, and this Muslim or Croat that they would have in reserve, so to speak, could later on serve to speak on the person's behalf and say that they haven't done anything bad. For instance, you've had very bad people, villains, who always have a few people who will speak in their favour, although they have done bad things to dozens of people. So this is what you would call the person that they keep in reserve.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked again, as you were asked the first time you appeared in this court, about the authority of various people, Radic, Vukic, Kupresanin, and Brdjanin. I just want to stick with Brdjanin. When Brdjanin spoke in public, on the radio or on television, did he have authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question should include a time frame, because the indictment is time specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In 1992, please, sir, between April and September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he certainly did have authority because in those turbulent times when something is in the making, you take the most prominent people to present what your agenda is, and he was a prominent person and a popular politician among the Serbs at the time. And he certainly did have great authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked about the -- by Judge Janu again, and this is at page 64, about when these statements were being made about Muslims either staying -- non-Serbs either staying or leaving, whether the population -- the agencies for replacement, exchange of population were operation. And your reply was: "This would have been at the beginning of 1992. Yes, certainly." In fact, can you jump ahead, please, to the 27th of May entry in your diary. There's one aspect I left out, if you can look at it, the 27th of May, please. Yes, page -- it's -- the page in the translation is L0054912. Sir, it's quite a long way into your entry. You discuss -- if you find the bit where you refer to the Esad Midzic School.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead with your question. I will be meanwhile looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, because you record -- it's a very simple point. You record there that Brdjanin had announced on Krajina news that Muslims and Croats had to move out of Banja Luka so that refugees might have somewhere to be housed and a special organ has been formed within the Crisis Staff to work on population exchange.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I'm asking you from the beginning of 1992 until his announcement, is that the first time you can recall there was any kind of an agency for population exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly wasn't the first time because refugees were already arriving at the time, and a place had to be found for them to be put up at. So there was mention of them earlier, before the -- even before these April events, before the putsch that I talked about. Once they took over the power, people saw what was brewing, what was going to happen, and realising where this policy would lead, where this authority that has taken over the power in Banja Luka was going, they started leaving the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. Sorry, it's my fault. What I mean is I know -- we've heard evidence that people were leaving before this. But until the 27th of May, had there been an official agency of any kind set up to organise the exodus of non-Serbs and the influx of Serbs? Any government agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, for instance -- there was this agency receiving Serbs, and following the putsch, as I called it, which took place in April, Banja Luka was hermetically shut off. The people knew that there was no existence for them there, and certainly there must have been agencies where they went and -- because they decided to renounce on all of their property. I, for instance, had to renounce some of my property, even people were asked to sign a paper saying that they're leaving their house to the state in order to be able to leave. I luckily did not have to do that. I left my apartment fully furnished, and it all remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll leave this topic, because it's there for all to see anyhow. I just want to deal with, then, please with the number of times we see Mr. Brdjanin appearing. Tuesday, you record him appearing on the 5th of May. If you go, please, to the following day, the 6th of May, do you record in your diary another press conference with Brdjanin, page -- I think that's the 6th of May. If we go to the following day -- I'm sorry, that was the still the 6th of May. Another press conference, L0051714, and this is where Brdjanin is informing journalists about the decisions which must be implemented. And then on the subject of the television programmes that you were talking about, could you go to the -- it's the same entry, the page is L0051717. It's the same day. Could you find, sir, in your original diary the part where you talked about a TV Novi Sad show. You were asked yesterday about TV --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th of May. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where you talk about a TV Novi Sad programme about the 1941 raid in Novi Sad when thousands of Serbs and Jews were killed in the most unscrupulous manner. "Again, pictures of terror and horror, suffering, tears and survivors' testimonies all over again. The documentary of the massacre continues after the news. The massacre in Backa followed by a conversation in the studio about the tragic event and the film. Guests in the studio include historian Zvonimir Golubovic and Dr. Raskovic." When they had these discussions, how did they deal with it? In other words, how were those events in these films you were seeing about 1941 dealt with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How were they dealt with? They started publishing documents and showing TV programmes featuring killed people, torched homes, and then these reputedly educated people give their comments on these footages, how Serbs are victims of torture and slaughtering and how they will be victimised. And the way I, as a viewer, see this is these people should know it because they're educated. They should know something about it. What they wanted to create was ethnic herds which would then set out to conquer whatever one thought belonged to him. This was the purpose that these programmes served, to transform the people into a herd that will follow its leader. Therefore, to avoid them -- to avoid them -- to prevent them to think with their own head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned today a gentleman named Borivoje Sendic, I think he's known as. Could you have a look at your diary for the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why did I have to write this much? Well, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it is at least a record, sir, of a turbulent year. 25th of May, the paragraph begins: "And who is Marko Beckovic"? Have you found --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Vesovic, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the top of that paragraph you talk about a journalist whose editor-in-chief is Miro Mladjenovic. "If Veljko Milankovic is to be believed, Milankovic was visited by members of Bosanska Gradiska Circle of Serbian Sisters." On the 24th --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "reported in yesterday's issue. He is a real soldier, I have to boast, says Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic, that I had two minister inside my unit. The then-ARKrajina Information Minister Miro Mladjenovic and Sendic, the forestry minister." Is that the same Sendic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladjenovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Sendic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the one and the same Miro Mladjenovic who was the editor of Glas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then Borivoje Sendic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Sendic was a member of one of these paramilitary units, and then forestry minister. It's one and the same person, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned Professor Lazarevic as a man of authority. Did Professor Lazarevic hold any political positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the president of the Serbian intellectuals in Banja Luka, that is the title he held. It seems so. He was sort of a leader of the entire group. I don't know which were the functions that he held, but he was extremely poisonous and open in his speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the gentleman whose nickname was Gugo, Gugo Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Predrag "Gugo" Lazarevic who became famous for saying that: "Today, people can be distinguished by their birth certificate."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Meaning what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meant that you are a person if you're an Orthodox, but you're not a person if you belong to any other faith or if you're a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally, on this replacement of Mladjenovic, could you have a look for a moment, please, at P2696, please. Didn't bring any exhibits with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably. We can make use of yours, Ms. Korner? Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm about to have the same problem. They don't have an exhibit that I need. They can't find it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you are still in time, Mr. Ackerman. Perhaps if you have a list of the exhibits you are going to need, we can do something about it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 2696 is with the registry. Correction, it is not with the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we make use of your document, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has been provided. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. It's bound to happen sometimes. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just have a quick look at that, read through that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember reading that at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely I read it at the time. I was interested in this, and I must have read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the English version of the document put on the ELMO, please, so at least we know what he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You also recorded entries in your diary about the removal of Mr. Mladjenovic and the speeches made by Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, they can be seen - I'm not going to put them up - on the 10th of August --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- and the 11th -- they are both on the 10th of August, so a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the reason -- can you now, without -- I don't want to show you the entries, but perhaps I can just lead on this because it's in the entries. Was the reason for his removal because it was felt that Glas was not properly reporting the SDS policies? Or one of the reasons anyhow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly so. But I think this was a matter of secondary importance. There were two groups of people who were basically stealing. They were grabbers, robbers. There was this group of Mladjenovic where this figure who was a criminal who was being promoted as almost a saint, whereas Veljko was here to protect Mladjenovic. These people felt the need to control this particular paper as well. This was a merciless struggle between two factions, let's put it that way. They all swore their allegiance to a Serbian ethnicity, to being Serb, but basically they were fighting and struggling for their own private interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. On that topic, then, there's a further Glas article, P291. Your Honour, I'll hand it, and we will put the other one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour. That's the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to suggest, Mr. Ackerman, that we have the break straight away so that we regroup the documents that you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are only two of them, Your Honour, and I have one of them here. So we're only missing one document. It's not that difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an article of Glas, 26th of July, so approximately ten days later. Could you turn it over, usher, because it's on the backside. The English I want turned over. "Where we see speaking of Banja Luka's intellectuals who had publicly protested against the town's current government, Brdjanin" -- I can't read that if you do that. I haven't got the contact lenses. Brdjanin said: `I believe that many at the Glas newspaper think the way I do. They're all Serbs, they all support the Serbian cause, but I cannot understand those who give so much space to the old defeated forces [the communists-- author's remark] in the paper for disseminating the communist notions of a so-called union and brotherhood and unity, even though it is evident that we can no longer coexist in this region." And then he goes on, "'What does Mr. Mico Carevic want? What kind of policy are he and other Banja Luka intellectuals pursuing?'" And then he goes on about the corridor, proof of the total genocide of the Serbian people is being prepared in Kozarac. Do you remember reading that article at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recall this title, the administrative board of Drnis, where it says that in almost 55 per cent of the companies, Croats and Muslims had been removed, dismissed. I think this is something that Brdjanin did talk about at the time. And this Cvijetic from Electronika, he criticised him for the fact he had people of other ethnicities in his company, in larger numbers than he should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The point I want to concentrate on at this moment is this: There Brdjanin seems to be saying that the paper or those who give so much space to the old defeated --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's pretty leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's true. I'm sorry, you're right. He's my own witness. I got so used to cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please rephrase your question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you help as to what Mr. Brdjanin was referring to there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he meant what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but what was he talking about: "I cannot understand those who give so much space to the old defeated forces." Are you able to assist on what he was referring to there? If not, say so straight away, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know what he was talking about. They were ostensibly all of them new democrats, but they were basically autocrats, and they transformed themselves into tyrants. All of this was old and bad for them. They were promoting new things that turned out to be far worse than the old things. And these were just phrases, hackneyed phrases that they were using. Well, you see, we were lead by those people and this is where they brought us to. This is the point where we are now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think I can take it much further. Thank you very much, sir. That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we have a break now or shall we start straight away? How long do you think you will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably about the same amount of time Ms. Korner did. Your Honour, the document is DB344. Nine copies of it were brought to this courtroom, three of them were given to you, to the Judges, one to the Prosecutor, one to the legal officer, one to the registry, for all the booths. Somewhere in this building we ought to be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can I please get a date for that document? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just to be real cautious, I think what I'll also do is send Mr. Vujic up to my flat to get a copy of it because it's important and I want to use it, and I have a right to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman is saying all this, Your Honour, for this reason, I sent an email this morning saying one of the documents I was going to object to was this particular document. And for the reasons I expressed, namely, that it's a part document, that we want to know where it came from, and we wanted the rest of the document, please, before it could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you're probably thinking about a different document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct. Which says "to be continued" and it starts in the middle of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At least that's some evidence that I brought it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I'd like the whole thing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They've got it, why didn't the registry have it? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. We got it from you a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have an exhibit number, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's DB344. It's on the exhibit list that I have given to you, and to the registry, and I have given the documents along with it. It's a mystery to me. That makes me think a lot of my exhibits have been just thrown away or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we'll track it down. We'll have a break, a 25-minute break starting from now. Can we reduce the break to 20 minutes. I just want to make sure that you have all the time you require, Mr. Ackerman, and that we will finish today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, nobody seems to want to bring Mr. Brdjanin back to Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours now have a copy of Mr. Ackerman's proposed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we do have a copy of Mr. Ackerman's DB344. But in the short time available I did try to see whether there is -- what the records are. There is a record of 343 being tendered and admitted, and 345, but not of 344. And it seems there was a question already when -- because you did --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a record of 343 being admitted because it's one of the other things I objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a record of 343 and 345 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because our records don't show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stick to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a very simple objection, as Your Honours can see, you don't need to read the whole thing. It's from, apparently, a publication called Patriot. The article is dated the 12th of August 2003. It's apparently part 2 of 9. We don't appear to have been provided with the other 7. As I understand it, Mr. Ackerman is putting it forward as the truth of the contents. You are to take, and the witness presumable is to take, as truthful, Mr. Sendic's account of events 11 years later. Your Honour, that's in our submission is objectionable. It's not a publication that came into being at the time of these events, unlike the other newspaper articles which we have put in and other articles which Mr. Ackerman has put in, which we have not objected to. If it is to be said that Mr. Sendic is to be looked for as a witness of truth or people are to be cross-examined on the basis that this is truthful evidence, then Mr. Sendic should be called as a witness. And that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little bit surprised you've asked me to respond to such a fatuous objection, but since you have, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You seem to be repeating what Ms. Korner said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I was. I didn't mean to be. Your Honour, I don't know if we're going to change the Rule, then of course I need to respond. But it was my understanding that documents are all admitted and that you sort them out in the end as to what weight they have or what value they have and that was my understanding. That's the way all the Prosecution's exhibits were admitted. I think I've objected to well over a hundred of them. They have all been admitted on the basis that you're professional Judges; you'll sort them all out, you'll look at them and say what the value is. I think if that rule is being changed, I think I can make an argument to the admissibility of this document. If it's not, then I really don't think I need to say more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you have to say about the point of Ms. Korner that this is only part 2 of a 9-part --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the rest of the parts are absolutely irrelevant to any issue in this case as near as I can tell. This is the only part of the whole thing that mentions Mr. Brdjanin and talks about a role that was played by Mr. Brdjanin with regard to this particular issue of paramilitary organisations. The rest of it is -- would just be surplusage in this record and would have no value to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a public source. The Prosecution can look at it and read it up to their heart's content, just like other public source documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do -- this is not in the same category, and Mr. Ackerman knows that full well, as any of the documents we've put in. What is objectionable is Mr. Ackerman presumably cross-examining the witness, say, on the basis this is a true, accurate, truthful account. This is one where it was open to Mr. Ackerman in his 65 list of witnesses, 65 witnesses on his 65 ter list to call. But if it's going to be cross-examined on the basis this is a truthful account, we have no way of disputing it without having the witness here. But it's wrong in our submission that it should be put to the witness that this is truthful. The most that can be said about this, this is somebody's account apparently written in a newspaper 11 years after the event, and may or may not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position as we see it as follows: We will allow this document to be admitted into evidence with the caveat that we have appended to several other documents and with the understanding that this is not to be presented to the witness as God's truth, as something which has been established, et cetera. It's just the opinion of the author and it has to be put to him as that. And with also the understanding that if a request is made for the tendering -- for the production of the rest of the article, in other words, part 1 and parts 3 to 9, because this is part 2 of 9 parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I formally make that request. I would like to be supplied with the other 9 parts of Mr. Sendic's remarkable account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other eight parts. Do you have the other eight parts, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we do. I don't want to represent we do. I think we have the issues of Patriot that have all those parts. But it is a public-source document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you understand because I'm not stupid, I'm not speaking to an inexperienced lawyer. If the witness in answering the question tells me: "Judge, this is only part 2 of a series of articles numbering 9, and I want to see the other 8 before I can give you my assessment," I'm not going to deprive him of that. And I can't. I simply can't do that. So please try to procure for us the remaining parts of the article. And we can admit the witness now, hoping that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Your Honour. I have another matter. I would like you to apply the same rule, Your Honour, to Prosecution's P2730 that was admitted today, because now there's a new rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which new rule, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The one you just announced. So I want the Prosecution to supply the real memorandum from the Serbian academy, not this Croatian piece of propaganda. If you look, Your Honour, at just the first page, 289 -- well, the first page says: "Roots of Serbian aggression." That's not in the original memorandum. The second page says: "All footnotes accompanying this text are by the editor." So it's been added to, so it's not the memorandum. It's some creation of some Croatian organisation to trash Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but again --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You let that you in without -- I objected. You let it in without any qualification at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Instead of grabbing the bull from the horns, you grabbed the bull from the tail, Mr. Ackerman. This is being presented for what it is, and it will taken for what it is. I think Ms. Korner is fully aware this is not the original and that it is being presented as a part of publication that comes from Zagreb. The weight that we will give it, we will tell you at the end of the story, not now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm perfectly happy if Mr. Ackerman tells me he has at home a Serbian copy of this, I'm perfectly content to ask to have his copied and we will replace the exhibit with the Serbian version. No objection at all. May I just mention one other thing, Your Honour, I think you will have to check your records if you were told that 345 had been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was told by my secretary, now ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can tell you, I know that's wrong because it purports to be a statement from General Talic signed on the 27th of December 2002. So I know for a fact that has never been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have seen it for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How it ever got admitted, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman still has the time to ask for the admission of those documents, those exhibits if they hadn't been admitted as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my plan is before I rest the Defence case is to request the admission of all the exhibits. And I'm not prepared to do that today, because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste more time. Let's bring in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if necessary, he can be here tomorrow, I have been told. He's not due to fly back until Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman will do us the favour of finishing with the witness in the three-quarters of an hour that we have. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, will you try to finish in three-quarters of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll will try. I won't guarantee that I can do it; I might not be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. In that case, we'll sit tomorrow morning. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sir, when you first started this morning, you had with you a little white notebook that I can see still sitting up there on the desk. I only have one question I want to ask you, and I do that with some hesitation. Can you tell me if Mr. Brdjanin's name appears anywhere in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it does not, or no, you can't tell me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's not there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really don't want to, and I'm glad you gave me that answer. You saved me that grief. You talked about Glas being -- the questions I'm going to ask you now are about some things you said today, and then we'll go into some things you said yesterday. You talked today about Glas being a racist newspaper. I want to know if you would describe, after a certain period, the newspaper Oslobodjenje as also being a racist newspaper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the period that is being discussed here, I cannot say anything specifically about Oslobodjenje because I did not have any opportunity to receive it. I haven't had any insight. In Banja Luka, you couldn't obtain it actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. You spoke today about an incident with a bus at Jajce and what was described as an ambush, and you were talking about the difference between the report that appeared in Glas and a report that appeared -- that was broadcast on Banja Luka Radio. And one of them talked about it as an ambush; one of them talked about it as a skirmish that broke out after the bus was stopped. Is that a fair statement of the two reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there were JNA reservists that were killed in that event, whatever it was, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Six reservists of the Yugoslav People's Army were killed, and one active policeman from the public security service from Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what you told the Chamber was that neither of the accounts, either the one in Glas nor the one on Banja Luka Radio, was the truth; that what had actually happened was that the JNA reservists had opened fire and other people had fired back. I think that's basically what you told the Chamber. And the first thing I want to ask you is, is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had the opportunity of meeting a man who happened to be on that bus. It was a regular bus line between Banja Luka and Bugojno. And when they were stopped for a regular checkup by the checkpoint in Jajce, then this policeman, I guess it was a Croatian policeman, boarded this bus, and then this man who was telling me about this said that this is when the reservists started shooting for some reason. And then these people, who were outside, started shooting at the bus. So that is how these casualties came about. Radio Banja Luka reported that there are six wounded persons, obviously civilians because there was no mention of reservists and they were transferred to the hospital in Jajce. That is what was written, too. Five were transferred to the hospital, but six were wounded. Five were transferred to the hospital in Jajce, and their lives were not in danger, so that was the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the story about what happened at the scene is a story that you got from somebody who claimed to have been there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A man who was there and who literally disappeared then. So everybody was worried where he was and what had happened to him. And he had actually gone to work somewhere on territory that was under Croatian control, if I'm not mistaken. And then he appeared much, much later and explained the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber his ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Serb. I'm sorry. As for the diary, I actually have what he gave me in writing about this particular event, but I cannot remember where it is right now. He wrote this in his very own hand, how all of this happened, where he was, why he did not call home, and that's why they thought that he had gone missing and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, do you not, that there was an official investigation of this incident, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that Glas wrote about it, and Radio Banja Luka said that an investigation was underway, but they did not provide any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 11 of today's transcript, you said this: "I looked at all the newspapers I could get my hands on." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about a newspaper called Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I don't. I just bought Glas actually. You see, at that time my pay was a disaster, my income was a disaster. I couldn't work. And a pack of cigarettes cost 500 million dinars. So I would just buy Glas every now and then; and if some friends would buy other newspapers, then they would bring them to me, and then I would read them very carefully. Of course, that includes Belgrade papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to restrict your answer for the question, because if you go beyond you will never finish. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see a newspaper called Kozarski Vjesnik? Whether you ever read one or not, did you ever see one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You told us that the Serbs were all armed, and you made this statement: "Even children had grenades." Did you ever personally see a child with a grenade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I didn't see any such thing. But for example, where children were throwing grenades in 1992 and 1993, that was shown then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shown where?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was shown where children were shown throwing grenades in 1992, 1993? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Children threw a grenade in front of Boska, and tens of passersby were injured. Glas wrote a lot about this. These were young boys, schoolboys.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was actually reported in Glas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember whether it was 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now. There has been too many things. I can't remember every detail. But it was in Glas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did a child throw this grenade, or did several children throw several grenades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think it was one grenade, one grenade. There were one or two boys, and they threw this one grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told this Chamber that "even children were armed with hand grenades," you were referring to this one incident where one child threw one hand grenade? And from that, you concluded that "even children were armed with hand grenades." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would like to correct this. Not grenades, one grenade. And children were armed. There are many examples that when they threw things like that, then somebody would lose an arm, somebody would lose a leg. Buzevic, Petricevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's answer Mr. Ackerman's question. Mr. Ackerman is suggesting to you that when you earlier on said that children were armed with hand grenades, what you actually had in mind or what you were basing your statement upon was only this one incident where only one child threw only one hand grenade, and there are no other instances of -- similar instances that you are aware of. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct. That is not correct. Children did have such things. Parents had such things. And children would secretly take them. And that is not the only case of a terrible thing like that happening because there was a grenade in a child's hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these cases of children with grenades were all reported in Glas, and that's how you know about them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know whether they were all recorded. I repeat once again, I did not get every copy of Glas. I heard of some cases. Friends told me about them. And then also the relatives of these children told me about such things, and also such things were written about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's jump to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you is this: I know you don't know Mr. Brdjanin. Let me ask you if you know that Mr. Brdjanin's two brothers are both married to women who are Croat. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, to tell you the truth, and I don't know why you're telling me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you another question: Did you know that Brdjanin's wife's family, there are mixed marriages involving Muslims? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I was not interested in Brdjanin's origins and in his life. I was interested in what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're going to be here in the morning if you continue to go beyond the answer. You answered the question that you didn't know about it. That was a complete answer. If you insist on going with these long answers, we will be here a long time because I have a lot of questions to ask you. We can do this quickly, or we can do it for a long time. I now want to ask you about the report that you heard that you said some people laughed at, that Brdjanin said: "We'll throw the children in the river, and if they swim out, they're Serbs". Don't you think, if it's true that he had all these mixed marriages in his life, that it's very unlikely that Mr. Brdjanin said such a thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Well, Hitler had Jewish blood in his veins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Is there a problem with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: None whatsoever, Your Honour. I'm just finding a place, because I want to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought there was a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to refer to a question and answer you were asked today. Judge Agius asked you, page 18, line 14, "do you recall ever having seen Mr. Brdjanin or having heard Mr. Brdjanin deal with the topic of these camps," referring to concentration camps, "of camps in general or in particular?" Your answer was: "No, no, I can't recall that." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, except what he said, we have the right to have camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, but when you were first asked the question, what you said was: "No, I can't recall that." Then the Judge say to you: "You don't recall Mr. Brdjanin being interviewed on TV, for example, on these camps?" And then you said: "Oh, yeah, I was wrong. He did say something once." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which line are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was one long answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't recall Mr. Brdjanin being interviewed on TV, for example, on these camps? Answer: "I cannot recall that." And then you said: "On one occasion, I think he said on television --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm reading it. Just wait. Give me a chance. "No, I don't think -- I'm sure he said on one occasion if the Russians and the Germans could have camps, why shouldn't we, the Serbs, be able to have camps. I think the broadcast was called Otvoreni Ekran," and then there's a caret, "or something like that." And then you said: "I think I heard that on one occasion." So you're just doing a lot of guessing there, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he said that. I did not say that I made a mistake. He did not talk about the camps or the actual establishment of the camps. I stand by what I said. I don't know that he said that. I do know if he said that Germans and Russians have camps, why would we Serbs not have the right to have them too. That he did say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But when the Judge asked you do you recall ever having seen Mr. Brdjanin or having heard Mr. Brdjanin deal with the topic of these camps, of camps in general or in particular, why did you tell the Judge that you couldn't recall it? Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that he talked camps in the sense of the actual establishment of the camps, the number of inmates, et cetera, if I have to clarify it. But that he did say at one point, if Germans and Russians, then why we Serbs not have them? I remember that. I remember he said that, and I saw that programme, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it being suggested that Mr. Brdjanin never said this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That he never said anything about Germans or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's being suggested that this witness never heard Mr. Brdjanin said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's different. So it's not being suggested Mr. Brdjanin never said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not conceding that Mr. Brdjanin ever said it. If that's what your asking for, you'll not get a concession from me about that. I'm just cross-examining the witness. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it needs to be clear. For a very clear reason, I think there's an exhibit on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is an exhibit on this. Let's not discuss in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to be absolutely clear that the suggestion being made to this witness is only that he never heard it, not that it was never said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness has just reiterated that he saw the TV programme himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm conducting a cross-examination, testing the credibility of the witness. That's all I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's why I'm allowing you to proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Question from Judge Agius about your diary of 28 August 1992, where you talked about Mr. Brdjanin being under a great deal of pressure, you told the Judge that a lot of people were coming to Mr. Brdjanin asking him for help, and you mentioned people from his community in Popovac that were coming and asking him for help. And that was, in fact, true. I mean there were a number of coming to Brdjanin in the fall of 1992 requesting help, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think they came before that and after that, because if somebody is in a high position, who would not turn to him? I mean, they're not going to turn to me; they're going to turn to people who can do something for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, you could have answered the question by just saying "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And among the people that were coming to ask him for help were Muslims and Croats, and he was in fact helping Muslims and Croats on occasion, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know whether he helped them officially. On a personal basis, perhaps. I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like to -- this is a question that kind of baffles me. Because I've spent quite a bit of time in former Yugoslavia, and I am unable to tell the difference between Croats and Muslims and Serbs by looking at them. And is that because I'm an American and didn't grow up there? Can people who grew up there just immediately tell by looking at someone whether they're a Muslim or a Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Cannot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They cannot. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then answer this question for me, because this is what baffles me: You told the Judges that when the SOS was in town, they would stop Croats and Muslims and take jewellery and money from Croats and Muslims. How did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they know that they were Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rifles, Mr. Ackerman, rifles. Rifles and an ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So they would stop people who didn't have rifles and take their money and jewellery, no matter whether they were Muslims or Croats, no matter what they were? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They stopped everybody, Serbs included. But if you had the right kind of name on your ID, then you could go on. But then if you did not have the right name, then you would be mistreated. So then on the basis of these IDs, these personal documents that people carried around, they would see who was who. You were not allowed to move about without such IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that the SOS made 10 demands and 11 were implemented. Can you tell us the ten demands, and tell us what of those demands were implemented. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was demanded was carried out. Let's be clear about that. Please try to show some understanding and do not split hairs. I'm not sure that it was 10. Maybe it was 12. Maybe it was 13. But I mean, this staff that was formed, they met an extra demand, even one that was not put forth originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, but I want to ask you the question. Tell me the demands that you know that were carried out. Number one, what was carried out; number two, what was carried out. Tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say this ethnic levelling. I mean, that was carried out so well that even some Serbs lost their jobs because they were not good enough Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's one. What's another one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember all of them. I mean -- well, please, don't make me guess now. It was so long ago. But all of it is written down here. All of it was written down specifically, and now if you expect me after 12 years to know each and every one of their demands, well, sorry, but I don't have that kind of memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have them written in your diary, you have my authorisation to look at them and refresh your memory, and then you can answer Mr. Ackerman's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman should point him to the part of the diary. Otherwise, this is a truly unfair cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the witness is being asked actually to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no idea where it is in the diary. He said it in response to your question this morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be 3rd April, 4th April, 5th April. I don't think you need to look any further. That's speaking out of memory. I may be wrong, but I think -- I don't think I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you have the 10 points there, or 11 or 12, whatever the number is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here they are. Under 1, that's in the territory of the Banja Luka security centre, which covers a much wider area -- oh, excuse me. Should I repeat what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Do we have go through one by one, Mr. Ackerman, now that he has found them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only want him to tell me the ones that he knows that were carried out. He said there were 11. I want to know what those 11 are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go through them, sir. And you can refer to the entry, the date, and then draw the conclusion ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, for instance, the demand to prosecute war profiteers, looters, and deserters once their actions came out into open and their names were known. This demand was put forward and adopted, but these people were never actually arrested. Under 4, the request for the removal in the banks --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me stop you on that. That's the second one. That's the request to prosecute war profiteers -- just let me finish my question. The request to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- And with regard to that one, Mr. Brdjanin agreed with that and supported that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's two. Now we talked about staff levelling, and we talked about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was under number 3. That was number 3, concerning the profiteers. Number 2 was something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. What was number 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2 was that the deadline was very tight. They were supposed to do it by 16th of April, Monday, for the people to sign the loyalty oath, of loyalty to Republika Srpska. I think this was about the insignia that was being imposed on the police. This was a way of forcing the Muslim and Croat members of the police to put on these new insignia and to sign an oath of loyalty to Republika Srpska if they wanted to continue working for the police. That was under 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have number 1 there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started reading out. It goes as follows: "In the territory of Banja Luka of the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka," which does not cover only the town of Banja Luka but a much broader area, "the law on internal affairs of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina should be made effective henceforth, the insignia should be changed, the cadres loyal to Republika Srpska -- to the Serbian Republic and Yugoslavia should be allowed to continue working," and it went on to say that this should be implemented in the territory of Bosnian Krajina. So the first part concerned the loyalty oath. Then under 2, it said that all of this had to be implemented by the 6th of April. So they were writing this on the 5th of April, and they wanted the deadline to be the 6th of April. It all had to be done quickly. Then the request concerning war profiteers. Then the request concerning dismissals in the banks, in the Privedna Banka in Banja Luka, the commercial bank, for the alleged action against the monetary putsch. And this request should also be implemented by the 6th of April 1992, before the crisis staff. And then conclusion number 5, or their request number 5, "we request the removals to be effected in the post office where" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it going to change history, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move ahead. Thank you for understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're going on another subject now, sir. You can put that away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th request is the most significant one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm trying to get you on the plane tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's not going until Saturday anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to get this finished. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said -- you were asked by Judge Janu about Alija Izetbegovic. You indicated that you believed that maybe he had made some mistakes. Do you think rejecting the Lisbon Peace Accords was a mistake that he made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall the instant peace accords, and I simply do not recall him rejecting any peace accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by the Judge about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge Agius.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- about the electronic media that could be watched and heard in Banja Luka. And you listed some. You didn't list Zagreb Television, but then today when the Judge asked you about it, you included Zagreb Television, that you could watch that on occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With snow on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With snow on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's also the case, isn't it, that you could listen to Radio Zagreb any time you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I probably misunderstood the Honourable Presiding Judge. I supposed he had asked me about the Banja Luka media, and that is what my answer was in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Banja Luka media would not include Novi Sad and would not include the Belgrade paper, Belgrade TV and -- but anyway. You've made your point, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, in that same conversation you were having with the Judge, you talked about a journalist named Risto Djogo on Pale TV, and you said he was guilty of shameful primitivism. Could you elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean by shameful primitivism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean by shameful primitivism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was such a base level of his reports. His reports served to offend members of other ethnic communities. This was the worst thing you could experience in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. On the other side, there were bad journalists as well. For instance, Smiljko Sagolj on the Croat side, but none of them reported in such a primitive, savage way as Djogo did. And in the end, he was killed by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was he on frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Constantly. He was the main attraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, 1993. I think ever since the Pale television was put into place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was it such a main attraction that people on the streets and in the coffee bars in Banja Luka talked about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, definitely. Those people who were more properly behaved, they would be ashamed of it. An intellectual of mine, a Serb -- a friend of mine, an intellectual, a Serb, he was ashamed of it. Others saw it as a joke, would laugh at it. There was this once when he placed a pistol against his forehead, and then fired. But of course, there was no bullet inside. And he said: "Well, I'm sorry to have disappointed you, Alija."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you say that he was frightening people, that he was frightening Muslim and Croat people with the things that he was saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was disgusting, and it is really sorrowful that something like this could have happened. You could imagine the level of behaviour where you have this man take up a Muslim flag, throws it on to the floor in the TV studio, and then stamps on it. That's terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But my question is was this disgust, shameful primitivism that this guy was engaging in on a daily basis and that people were talking about, was it frightening people? Was it causing them to be afraid? Especially Muslims and Croats, was it frightening them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have answered this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, you haven't. Was it frightening people? You can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have frightened you to see the kind of people you had in power, someone who could just come up to you, hit you on the head and do whatever he felt like doing to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your answer is yes, in other words, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just say yes or no because you keep going around in circles without answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Another subject, now, you were aware, weren't you, that there were Croats and Muslims who continued to serve and sit in the Banja Luka Assembly throughout the war? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if I suggest to you that Mr. Brdjanin was never on Belgrade or Pale television in 1992, could you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really, but I will not claim to the contrary. I wouldn't be able to do that. The TV Novi Sad is a branch TV studio of the Belgrade television. And he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm contending and suggesting to you that he was never on -- in 1992, that he was never on television in Belgrade or Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He told you that. He said he doesn't agree, but he can't prove to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When Ms. Korner was asking you questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the witness is trying to finish the question. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think the witness ought to be allowed to say whatever he wants to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine with me. I'm just trying to get us finished by seven. If he wants to stay till tomorrow ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have anything else to say? I think you have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can prove that he was on the TV Novi Sad show. That was after the proclamation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know what date it was because it wasn't really important for me, but he was certainly there. Him, Vukic, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At some point during your testimony, and I neglected to write down when it was, you talked about the conditions that people were living under, and you said that people could not afford newspapers. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that time, a lot of news was travelling among people just by word of mouth, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. My copy of Glas, if I bought it, for instance, it would be read by 50 people. And we watched the radio and TV by switching on to the car battery. And they kept repeating news reports in order for the people who sometimes didn't have electricity to be able to hear it as well when they do have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You might have misunderstood my question. So let me ask it in a different way just to be sure your answer is to what I ask. What I'm suggesting to you is one of the ways the people learned what was happening was by hearing about it from other people. News was travelling from person to person by word of mouth, in other words. Even if they weren't reading the newspaper, they were learning about things by people telling them about them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one way, but I, however, did not use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware -- well, your diary is full of things that people told you. What do you mean you didn't use it? Your diary's full of people telling you things that you wrote down in your diary. That's word of mouth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you did use it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, but whenever I wrote down the name of the person who had been beaten up, I would also write down his ID number and the source from whom I got the information. And if I happened to be wrong, I would subsequently go back to this entry and change it accordingly and say that they didn't give me the right information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering the question, and I think we can move to the next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where you are aware that 1.860 Muslims in Celinac had their lives saved by Mr. Brdjanin? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object to that characterisation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He might have, if he had sent them out of Celinac and saved them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object to that characterisation, Your Honour. The evidence shows that the Muslims left. There's no evidence that their lives were saved by Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's direct evidence. A witness said those exact words. Exact words, a Muslim witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Please, please, please. Are you aware, sir, of any event in which Mr. Brdjanin was involved as intervening on behalf of -- Mr. Ackerman said 1.800 Muslims in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 1.860, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 60.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish I did, but I do not. But believe me, if the people went out of there, he did save them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence, not your opinion, not your guessing, not your speculation, do you have any evidence that Mr. Brdjanin was a thief, a robber, or a war profiteer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When would you say the largest number of Serbs left Banja Luka? I'm sorry, the largest number of non-Serbs. When would you say the largest number of non-Serbs left Banja Luka? What year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in this period we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. During the war period. What year during the war period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some time in the beginning of 1993, up until the end of 1993. That's when people started leaving en masse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, page 29 and 30, I believe it was, of the transcript,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS ASKED YOU THIS
utterances.text: "How frequent, according to your -- according to you were these statements in the local media labelling Muslims as Islamic fundamentalists, extremists or fanatics and can you recall specific instances?" And your answer, line 14: "Yes, I think I can, Your Honour. This was a common occurrence, an everyday phenomena. Everyday." Now, I'd really like to know if you mean that it was an everyday occurrence. I mean, can you look in your diary and show us every day in your diary that there was some statement about labelling Muslims as extremists or fanatics? Does that appear every day in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to a large extent, yes, I can. Although I would only write it down once, this would be heard every day. And then if I heard something new in their announcement, I would write it down. Yes, but I do know that this was an everyday occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were selective about the things you wrote in your diary, of course, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are aware of the fact that this isn't so. What I meant to say was that it was unnecessary for me to repeat the same story all over again every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. But it was you who selected actually at the end of the day whether this was worth reporting in your diary or not. This is what is being suggested. When you decided to make an entry, you made an entry. When you decided it was not the case of making an entry, it did not make an entry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, prior to every news report Krajiski Dnevnik, the pronouncement would be broadcast, and they would repeat the same thing. And I felt unnecessary to write down every day one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are talking at cross-purposes. And I also think, if I remember well, Mr. Ackerman, that he did mention after all that he was not buying Glas on a daily basis because he couldn't afford that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only point I want to make, Your Honour, is that he was selecting. And I think you made the point for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The point has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you this, now, page 33 it's your further answer to Judge Agius regarding that issue. It says: "Here, for instance, I'm looking at a declaration, which says: 'Serbs and all honourable Krajina people, let us stand up and defend our freedom, our religion, and our homes. We are fighting against Ustasha and Islamic fascists. We are fighting lies and international conspiracy. We're fighting for the truth, and we cannot lose.'" Who said that? Who does your diary indicate said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an announcement that was broadcast before and after the Banja Luka Radio news. I wrote this once, and I could not write the same thing every time after I had heard the news. Not that I avoided writing something down, I would write something new if I heard it. But I felt it unnecessary to write this same stuff every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. And that was -- so it's your position, then -- and I'm not sure I disagree with you. It's your position then that it was a daily announcement that you could hear on Banja Luka -- was it radio or TV? Radio.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I think it was a radio announcement. I think so. But it does say here, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that wasn't something Mr. Brdjanin was saying; that's something the announcer on the radio was saying I think you said before every newscast?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For God's sake, it was an announcement, or even a radio jingle if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Common. If you were paying attention to the radio, you couldn't have missed it. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said then also the following: "Let us understand. We are not under the blockade by the 6th American fleet, but by the -- Zulja and Mulja from Gracac town" and something and something. The transcript doesn't reveal what you really said. "May they all die or get killed by a bullet. That is the kind of justice they all deserve." Was that a daily thing you'd hear on the radio, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment I heard it, I wrote it down. This was one of the announcements. You can see the level of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I can, but that's not Mr. Brdjanin saying that, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For God's sake, I didn't even write it down as Mr. Brdjanin having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do you really think that I should attribute to him things in addition to what he actually did say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
