utterances.text: You were asked yesterday a lot about Mr. Brdjanin's statements and speeches and the effect of those speeches. And on page 34, line 8 through 19, the Judge asked you if you could provide specific instances of -- let me find the exact... "Relative to the period" - I'm on page 34 - "April 1992 to December 1992, are you aware of any incidents occurring as in your mind a direct link or a direct result of what was stated in the media? Please be specific. I don't want you to be generic because being generic doesn't help us in the least." And then you said had you known this would be asked, you would have taken some time in the hotel to look at the entries. And the Judge said maybe you'll have time later this evening and tomorrow morning to see if you can find any of these instances and come back to us tomorrow. Did you find any specific incidents occurring as a direct link to things stated in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war itself is a direct consequence. I apologise. I dedicated myself to the topics raised by the Honourable Judge; Mladjenovic and others. That's what I looked up. I'm sorry to say I didn't look up this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The one I just mentioned was a topic raised by the Honourable Judge. He asked you to look at it last night. And the answer is you haven't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I do have it in writing here what the Presiding Judge had said, and I wrote it down. And I didn't have this among my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He may have been misled by --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know exactly what happened. You gave him the instructions at the very end what you were going to bring up, and it wasn't among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As you sit here right now, can you tell this Trial Chamber of one incident, a crime, a war crime, that you can connect with any statement that you contend was made by Radoslav Brdjanin? Just one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I can remember, whatever the events I remember, I think that Brdjanin has was played a role in it. But now you're asking me to say whether I think that whatever happened had actually been impacted upon by what Mr. Brdjanin had said, and I cannot claim this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned to us yesterday that Mr. Brdjanin said something about "strike them off the soles of our feet." I wonder if you have seen the videotape --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wonder if you have seen the videotape of the exact language that was used by Mr. Brdjanin in the speech in which something like that was said. Have you seen that videotape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have. That borders should be established, yes. I've seen that tape, and that we should free ourselves of the pagans and the heathens, and these are Mr. Brdjanin's words. After all, the videotape exists, and it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll suggest a number of things to you. First of all, there's nothing in that tape about pagans and heathens. I suggest that to you. I suggest to you that that tape is from 1993, and that it was made in the context of the Vance-Owen Plan and the referendum on that plan, and that what Mr. Brdjanin said, in effect, was that if the cantonisation that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I specifically, and my two colleagues specifically avoided referring the witness to that particular tape, as you may have noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably for that reason. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would suggest that -- I don't want to stop you if you want to continue asking the question on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm fine with what you just said, Your Honour. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your prior testimony here, on 24 June at page 18.167, and you were asked about this statement yesterday, so you heard it yesterday, you said "most of the fatal decisions, at least the way it seemed, were taken by Brdjanin." I wonder if you can name one decision that was made in 1992 by Brdjanin. One decision of any kind, just one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the SOS announcement which had been read out by him. The radio presenters read out the announcement, and he talked about these -- the conclusions adopted by the staff in response to these requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's conclusions adopted by a crisis staff. I asked you if you could give us one decision that was taken by Brdjanin, not by some staff, a decision taken by Brdjanin. Do you know one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think yesterday he explained that statement, Mr. Ackerman, by practically rephrasing it and saying that this was a perception that one could have had because he was the one who was announcing all these decisions. But then he specifically stated that he didn't mean to say that these decisions were actually taken by him, by your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that's what you heard, Your Honour, and that's the record, then I'm satisfied with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know what you want to do, Your Honour. I've got. I don't think I have more than ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will avoid us having to come tomorrow. Okay? Yes, I am so grateful. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, try to restrict it as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Miro Mladjenovic, did you know that he was not a trained journalist and that he was -- I'm not sure about that. Did you know that he was put in the editor's position of Glas by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was an untrained journalist. Yes, I know that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you know that he was put in his position as editor by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presumed so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that he participated in the capture of the transmitter at Mount Kozara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He and Andjelko Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to refer to some entries in your diary of the 15th of July 1992. That's the one that has been referred to before where you actually said you dialed a number and talked to him. And I'm looking on -- it's page 4 of the English, L0048330. It talks about Kupresanin, Brdjanin, and Vukic trying to remove Mladjenovic from his position as editor in chief at Glas. And you say this: "The epilogue of these attempts by the aforementioned three officials happened at the session of the Crisis Staff subsequently renamed War Presidency of the region on 6 July when the conclusion was passed that the leading person of the paper should be removed." Now, as a matter of fact, Mladjenovic ignored that decision and took the position that the Crisis Staff had no power to remove him, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you also know that he took the position that the Crisis Staff did not have the power to remove him, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my position about it. He did have the opinion that you mentioned now. But he had to actually leave in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he had to leave because what he said was that the crisis staff didn't have any authority to take that position and to replace him, that only the municipal assembly, the founder of the paper, had that power. He said -- and it's in your diary; I'm now on page 6 of the English -- that the war presidency of the AR Krajina passed another conclusion. Without any authority whatsoever, the war presidency decided, among other things, to appoint some other people in his place. The conclusions show the war presidency claims competencies it does not have as these competencies belong exclusively to the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly, the founder of the aforementioned media. So he ignored them until it was the municipal assembly that replaced him. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to you look at a document marked Defence Exhibit DB344. This comes from a publication called Patriot, and it's from 12 August 2003 edition of Patriot. Are you familiar with that publication at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like you to notice is it was written -- the article that you have before you, the section of it, was written by -- apparently by Boro Sendic, who we have talked about earlier today. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This was published after I had left Banja Luka. This is why I'm not familiar with it. As far as I see, this is December 2003. I left in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: December or August?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The only question I want to ask you, and it's simple but it's going to require you to do a little bit of reading. If you go to the last --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: December.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. -- the last page of this document, sir, you'll find a paragraph that begins -- my Serbo-Croat isn't great. But if you start where it says "hoce mogu smiju," and read down to the end, "Radovana," you'll see the material I'm interested in. Do you see where I'm looking? You'll see Vojo Kupresanin's name, Stojan Zupljanin's name, and Radoslav Brdjanin's name, as you read through there, and Grahovac is there, too. If you read that section, I'll ask you just one question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was this -- the municipal assembly was called on the 15th of November by Vojo Kupresanin? Is that the part you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. If you start there with "calling a meeting of the assembly by Vojo Kupresanin..."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And read on down until you get to the end of the publication. It's fairly short. You can actually skip a lot and go from the last time you see "Zupljanin" down to the next time you see "Grahovac," if you want to. So what you should have read up there where it says 15 November, that: "Assembly vice-president Brdjanin attacked Grahovac. What did he think he was doing setting up some paramilitary unit without consulting the assembly, spending money on it, buying uniforms and so forth, with Sendic and Mladjenovic? He sent them across the River Sava without anyone's approval, and what were they doing there"? And then if you go down to the end, Sendic says: "The assembly did not decide on anything. Brdjanin's proposal that the three of us be charged for harmful and inappropriate behaviour was not accepted." Do you see all that? And the only question I have, which might make this easy for you, is sitting there in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- did you learn about this? Were you aware that this had happened? Did you have any knowledge of this before I showed it to you today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about this. This was published in December. I had already left Banja Luka by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm asking you. I'm not asking if you knew about this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the question should be phrased differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking if you knew anything about the events --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know about the events that are described in this article, in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ever heard of any such events? Ever heard of any such events?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 1991. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know anything about Brdjanin being opposed to paramilitary groups and war profiteers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paramilitary groups. Did you know anything about him being opposed to paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he advocated SOS, and SOS is also a paramilitary organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know anything about him being opposed to war profiteers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we there, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, he spoke against war profiteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I need to go into private session, Your Honour, for one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Open session. Your Honours indicated you would be letting both of us, both sides, know of matters we should address in our final briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have already drafted it. We are in the process of, you know, doing some further thinking to see whether we should add anything on them. But it's a matter -- I think you will have it first thing next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being drafted already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Once more, I should like to thank the interpreters, not only for the high quality of your interpretation. Today in particular, I was really impressed at a particular moment what a high level of interpretation we were receiving. But I also want to thank the technicians, the Registrar, the deputy, all the staff, and you, Mr. Ackerman, for finishing as you promised, and you, Ms. Korner, for your cooperation. Thank you. Thank you, sir, for coming again. I know it wasn't easy, but I should like to thank you. And above on everyone once more, I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you. And I would also like to thank the interpreters for having interpreted my words, despite the fact that I sometimes spoke very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.
